To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the required properties of magnetocaloric materials for magnetic refrigeration are: adiabatic temperature change larger than 2.35 of the currently existing materials, transition temperature between 40 and 50 degrees Celsius, and mechanical properties comparable to the existing materials.

the required properties for magnetocaloric materials for magnetic refrigeration are a transition temperature in the range 30–50 °C, adiabatic temperature change larger than 15 K, and a magnetic field strength of 0.5 T.

the magnetocaloric effect is not large enough in currently existing magnetocalorics, that materials with adiabetic entropy change 2-3 times larger than the currently available ones are needed to out-perform vapor-compression refrigeration technology, and that the magnetocalorics should be able to operate in the temperature range 20-40 °C.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of magnetocaloric materials for the application of room-temperature magnetic refrigerator.
the material requirements for magnetic refrigerators.
the development of new magnetic materials for room-temperature magnetic cooling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the existing magnetocaloric material is far from being suitable for commercial magnetic refrigerator applications, and a lot more effort is needed to improve the performance of the existing materials or find new materials with better properties.

a material with a magnetic transition temperature of 30–40 °C with an adiabatic temperature change of 10 °C at an applied magnetic field of 1.5 T is needed to make a magnetic refrigerator competitive with a vapor-compression refrigerator.
the magnetocaloric material requirements for the investigated cases are: adiabatic temperature change 2.5 times higher and adiabatic heat capacity 2.35 higher than the existing materials.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current state-of-the-art magnetocaloric materials do not have the required properties to outperform vapor compression systems.
for magnetic refrigeration to be commercially viable, the materials need to have adiabatic magnetocaloric effect 2.35 larger than the current materials.
for magnetic refrigeration to compete with vapor-compression, materials with a larger adiabatic magnetocaloric effect and better mechanical properties are needed.

the current research on magnetocaloric materials is not sufficient to meet the requirements needed for commercial magnetic refrigeration.
